nameStory: The Giant Lichen Orbweaver gets its name from two key features: its impressive size compared to many other orbweavers, and its masterful camouflage that mimics the mottled gray-green patterns of tree lichens. When resting on bark during the day, this spider practically vanishes, looking exactly like a patch of crusty lichen growing on the tree trunk.
description: The Giant Lichen Orbweaver is a large, robust spider that creates classic circular webs between trees and shrubs. Its body displays beautiful mottled patterns in shades of gray, brown, and greenish hues that provide excellent camouflage against lichen-covered bark. Females can grow quite large with thick, sturdy bodies, while males remain much smaller. This is one of the more impressive orbweavers you'll encounter in New England forests.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Distinctive mottled gray-green pattern on the abdomen that looks exactly like tree lichen - rough, patchy, and multi-toned with irregular light and dark blotches

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Large, perfect circular orb web typically spanning 12-18 inches, with sticky spiral threads that feel slightly tacky when accidentally touched

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Females have thick, robust bodies that feel substantial if gently captured - noticeably larger and chunkier than most other orbweavers

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Rounded, bulbous abdomen that appears almost swollen, with a relatively small head region and sturdy legs

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often sits motionless on tree bark during day, pressed flat against the surface where it becomes nearly invisible

habitat: Found in mature deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly where lichen-covered oak, maple, and birch trees are common. Prefers areas with moderate canopy cover that provide both sunlight for web-building and shaded bark surfaces for daytime hiding. Often encountered along forest edges and woodland trails where trees are spaced for optimal web placement.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin appearing in late spring, with females starting to build their first webs of the season in sunny forest openings.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when large webs are most visible and adults are actively hunting. Mating occurs during mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Females create egg sacs in early fall before the first frost. Adult spiders become less active as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off after first hard freeze, with eggs overwintering in protected locations under bark or in leaf litter.

funFact: This spider is such a lichen mimic that researchers have found them resting on artificial structures painted to look like bark - they seem to choose their hiding spots based on visual pattern matching rather than actually detecting real lichen.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Marbled Orbweaver, but the Giant Lichen Orbweaver's pattern looks specifically like crusty tree lichen (rough and patchy) while the Marbled Orbweaver has smoother, more flowing marbled patterns. Memory trick: 'Lichen' sounds like 'liking' rough bark!
compareHints: Among the Araneus orbweavers, the Giant Lichen Orbweaver stands out for its specific lichen-mimicking camouflage, while relatives like the Cross Orbweaver have distinct white cross markings and the Marbled Orbweaver displays smooth, flowing color patterns. The Barn Orbweaver tends to be more yellow-orange, lacking the gray-green lichen tones that make this species so distinctive.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its cousin the Marbled Orbweaver which has swirled, mottled patterns, the Cross Orbweaver's white cross marking is clean and distinct.

Among New England's Araneus orbweavers, the marbled orbweaver is unique for its extremely inflated, almost spherical abdomen—much rounder than the Cross Orbweaver's more egg-shaped belly or the Shamrock Orbweaver's triangular markings.

Among its Araneus cousins, the barn orbweaver is distinguished by its strong preference for wooden human structures, while the cross orbweaver favors gardens and the marbled orbweaver prefers trees and shrubs.

Among its Araneus cousins, the shamrock orbweaver's white spots make it relatively easy to distinguish - the cross orbweaver has a distinctive white cross pattern, while the marbled orbweaver shows complex marbled coloring without distinct dots.

Nordmann's Orbweaver is generally less distinctively marked than its famous cousins like the Cross Orbweaver (which has a prominent white cross pattern) or the Marbled Orbweaver (with its striking yellow and black marbled appearance).

Among its Araneus relatives, the Fierce Orbweaver stands out for its bold behavioral responses rather than distinctive markings like the Cross Orbweaver's white cross or the Marbled Orbweaver's marbled patterns.

Among its Araneus relatives, the Lattice Orbweaver's crosshatch pattern sets it apart from the distinctive white cross of the Cross Orbweaver and the swirled, marble-like patterns of the Marbled Orbweaver.
Unlike the Cross Orbweaver which prefers gardens and woodland edges, or the Marbled Orbweaver found on trees, the Openfield Orbweaver specifically chooses exposed grasslands and meadows.

Among its Araneus relatives in New England, the Red-spotted Orbweaver is most easily distinguished by its reddish markings - the Cross Orbweaver has a white cross pattern, the Marbled Orbweaver has marbled yellow and brown coloring, and the Shamrock Orbweaver has a distinctive shamrock-like pattern.

Among the many Araneus orbweavers in New England, the Butterfly Orbweaver stands out for its wing-like geometric patterns rather than the cross-shaped markings of the Cross Orbweaver or the marble-stone appearance of the Marbled Orbweaver.
Among its many Araneus relatives in New England, the Juniper Orbweaver's defining characteristic is its habitat specialization rather than distinctive markings.

Unlike the Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross pattern on the back, or the Marbled Orbweaver with its orange and white marbled appearance, the White-bellied Orbweaver's key feature is underneath rather than on top.

Among its Araneus cousins in New England, the Red-backed Orbweaver's bright green front section makes it stand out from the typically brown or gray Cross Orbweaver and the yellow-and-black patterned Marbled Orbweaver.
Distinguishing Araneus iviei from its many orbweaver relatives in New England requires expert knowledge, as most species in this genus share similar web-building behavior and general body structure.

Unlike the common Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross marking, or the Marbled Orbweaver with its mottled, marbled pattern, the Black-spotted Orbweaver displays clear black spots as its defining feature.

Unlike the abundant Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross marking, or the variable Marbled Orbweaver with its yellow and black patterns, Araneus bonsallae lacks well-documented field marks for New England populations.

Unlike the common Cross Orbweaver with its white cross markings or the Marbled Orbweaver with its yellow and black patterns, the Humped bog orbweaver's most distinctive feature is its physical shape rather than its coloration.
